comments.text: I used to work on a great white shark research boat in South Africa- I absolutely love those animals! The "punch it in the nose" idea is circulated a lot about what to do in the case of a shark attack. The odds of anyone being in this situation are tiny, but IF you are: the gill slits are actually the more sensitive area that you want to aim for, especially since if you aim for the nose you might end up with your hand in the shark's mouth! However, there's one thing about this that no one thinks about: ever tried punching something underwater? Doesn't work too well.
comments.author: @ekbrandon93

comments.text: 2:30 A woman I went to college with was swimming next to her dad's sailboat (she was 12 at the time) when a speedboat raced by their boat. She knew they wouldn't see her and so tried her best to dive under the water as deep as possible. But she didn't quite make it and the propeller pulled her legs up and sliced them to ribbons. Luckily she was able to get to a hospital in time, but she said every day for two weeks, doctors and her parents would come in at least once a day and tell her they needed to amputate her legs. She was 12 and very stubborn, so she kept telling them, "No, I'm going to walk again. Just wait." After two weeks she did start to heal much better and the blood supply to her legs and feet recovered after many surgeriess. Eventually she did walk again. She still had horrible scarring on both legs and sometimes wore a brace on one or both legs to relieve the pain - partially because she later got in a terrible crash while riding on the back of a Vespa at age 18. Girl was unstoppable because she did the physio and recovered from that, too.

12:20 Ciguatera toxins also cannot be destroyed by cooking, so there is no way to make the fish that has Ciguatera toxin edible for humans. It doesn't affect the fish so they just eat each other without issues. But it accumulates up the food chain, until it reaches lethal levels and makes the fish inedible for humans.

There is a unconventional way to detect ciguatera when eating high risk fish like barracuda and other predator fish higher up the food chain. You cut a filet of the fish and leave it out in the open to see if insects like flies will eat it. If it is left untouched by insects even after several minutes, it most likely has the Ciguatera toxin and is inedible.

comments.text: 11:21 I had a mild case of ciguatera once after eating a small moray eel while fishing in the Tropics. I experienced indigestion and diarrhea, flulike symptoms, and I did have a reversal of hot and cold sensations, which was the weirdest thing. Luckily my symptoms wore off completely after a few days, probably due to eating only a smaller amount of contaminated fish. I didn't need medical treatment, but prepared myself to seek it if the symptoms had gotten worse. As the clip says, the thing to do is avoid eating reef predators especially, like morays, barracudas and grouper, or any such predators that are higher up in the food chain, because the ciguatoxin usually accumulates in the food chain of shallow coastal waters, where the dinoflagellate microorganisms mainly occur that produce the ciguatoxin. On the other hand, deep sea fish or herbivorous coastal fish are usually safe to eat even in areas where ciguatera poisoning occurs.

comments.text: An important bit of information that I haven’t seen anyone talking about pertaining to the fourth video - if you’re in the water and you see a shark, DO NOT SPLASH AROUND AND PANIC!!! This will only draw more attention to you and make the shark more likely to try and bite you, because you’re triggering it’s hunting drive. It’s important to stay calm and try to get away as quickly as possible, and if it approaches you and looks like it’s going to bite you, jab (not punch) at the gills/eyes to deter it. NEVER splash and scream.

13:50 - People really do underestimate hypothermia.

Years ago I nearly went hypothermic in the middle of august, in the UK. I was working at an equestrian centre at the time and was on the afternoon/evening shift, weather was absolute shite as usual for the UK. it was maybe 15 degrees but had torrential rain and gale force winds. I was okay for a while when I was working, but my family who was due to pick me up had gone for food in a nearby restaurant. I then had to sit outside for a couple of hours soaked through to the skin because no one was even picking up the phone.

It really made me appreciate how dangerous it can be. I've never felt that cold. By the time I did get in the car I was shaking uncontrollably. At least that was a good thing but I was just so cold.... and that was SUMMER, wet and on land. In the water is so much worse.

comments.text:
When people are in the water on boards, and their legs are dangling, sharks can mistake them for other animals like seals as their eyesight isn’t the best. They see a rounder body and legs and think it’s their food choice, however when they bite into the person they don’t like the taste and tend to spit them out, which is why body parts can be found in the water after attacks. In Hawaii around Hanauma Bay, body parts would wash up from bites.
